1.pericope_label: I will praise thee, O Lord, with my whole heart: the vow of praise, and the riddle of the title

schools.summary: Gill insists the verb means to confess and declare openly in the congregation, so that this is vocal singing with the heart joining rather than mental singing, and lists what the rejoicing is not in; Calvin takes the whole heart for an upright heart against a double one, turns it into an indictment of men who acknowledge God once and then sing triumphs to their own valour, and argues that the psalm as a whole is a prayer that recalls many past deliverances rather than a thanksgiving for one victory.

Henry calls the title a very uncertain sound, inclines to read it as a tune, and has the joy pass through whatever occasions it and terminate in God rather than the gift; Spurgeon puts the argument in four words, that half heart is no heart, and holds that gratitude for one mercy refreshes the memory as to thousands of others.

Clarke gathers the ancient versions on the title, reports Houbigant’s re-division of the Hebrew into a word for hidden things, notes that several of the fathers took the phrase of the incarnation, and thinks it as painful as useless to follow every conjecture through.

Ellicott notes only that the alphabetic arrangement begins in its completest form, every clause of the first stanza opening with Aleph; Delitzsch rules out both the Greek rendering and Luther’s bolder one on the ground that the preposition occurs once in the text, and traces the Nabal reading revived by Hengstenberg to the same erroneous idea.

debates.question: What does the title of the psalm mean?

sides.position: a tune or an instrument, the occasion being the nations that opposed David’s settlement on the throne
the opening of a well-known song to whose tune the psalm was set
the death of the strong man who went out between the camps, that is Goliath
holders: the Chaldee, reported by Adam Clarke

sides.position: the secrets or the infancy of the Son, read by some of the fathers of the incarnation
holders: the ancient versions and Houbigant, reported by Adam Clarke

sides.position: all such conceits rest on an erroneous idea, the Nabal transposition included

debates.question: Is the psalm a thanksgiving for one victory?

sides.position: no: the greater part is praise, but the whole ought to be considered a prayer, in which many deliverances are recalled to open the gate of prayer for the trouble now upon him
it is a triumph in the defeat of the nations that opposed his settlement on the throne

outliers: Calvin alone turns the whole heart into a charge against victorious generals, who had solemn thanksgivings decreed in their names and abused them under a false pretence to get an opportunity for boasting.
Gill alone notes that the Chaldee makes the object of the rejoicing the Word.
themes: a title nobody can read
a heart undivided or not a heart at all
praise that must be told to others
joy that stops at the giver

3.pericope_label: Thou hast rebuked the heathen, thou hast destroyed the wicked: cities whose very memory is perished

schools.summary: Gill fills the clauses with instances, from the Philistines turning back at their champion’s death to the retreat of sin and Satan and antichrist, reports the Targum and Kimchi and Jarchi on who is meant by the heathen and the enemy, and settles on antichrist rather than Satan for the one addressed.

Clarke turns the turning back inward, as the sign of a nearly approaching conquest over sin, guesses the Canaanitish nations for the blotted-out heathen, and argues from the extinct Hivites and Perizzites that for ever and ever here has its proper sense of endless.

Ellicott works the stanza as grammar and text, allowing the opening clause to be temporal or causal or both, preferring stumble through weakness to fall, reading blotted out as a name erased from the civil roll, refusing the vocative in the last verse as unintelligible, and noting that the Daleth stanza is missing; Delitzsch reads the strophe letters structurally, takes the thanksgiving as the sum of many judgments rather than one, follows Hengstenberg in seeing the Amalekites beside the Ammonites, and makes the contrast with the abiding throne the strophe’s point.

debates.question: Who are the heathen whose cities are blotted out?

sides.position: the Canaanitish nations, whose extinction proves the phrase for ever and ever means endless
not the Philistines of the Targum and Kimchi, nor Jarchi’s Esau, nor Amalek, but antichrist and the antichristian states
the Ammonites, and at the same time the Amalekites, threatened since the time of Moses with a blotting out of their remembrance
no particular nation: the point is the evanishment of great cities from history, as with Sodom and Gomorrha

debates.question: Is the last verse of the stanza addressed to the enemy?

sides.position: no, the vocative gives no intelligible meaning; render it as a statement, the enemy is made an utter wreck and perpetual ruin
the verse is better re-rendered to the same effect, the enemy desolated for ever and his cities destroyed
the address stands, and the question is only who is addressed

outliers: Ellicott alone reaches outside the commentators for illustration, citing Shakespeare on the Judge whom no king can corrupt and Browning on a city turned overnight to ashes.
Ellicott alone records that the Greek and the Latin read with a sound in the last verse, which he takes for the crash of falling cities.
themes: enemies who stumble as they retreat
a throne occupied while cities fall
a name struck off a register
a missing letter in the acrostic

7.pericope_label: But the Lord shall endure for ever: a throne prepared for judgment and a refuge for the oppressed

schools.summary: Gill reads the enthronement as the unchangeableness and power of God and applies it to Christ, who sits King until his enemies are made his footstool, fixes the scope of the judgment from Ben Melech’s note that the word means the whole habitable earth, catalogues the oppressions the crushed must carry, and requires a knowledge of the name that is affectionate and experimental rather than notional.

Spurgeon argues from the past to the future, since the same Almighty fills the throne, takes the throne prepared for judgment as a promise about the swiftness of divine justice in a court where no suitor is worn out by waiting, and compresses the refuge into a line, that there were cities of refuge under the law and God is our refuge-city under the gospel.

Clarke makes providence as a whole founded in righteousness and truth, and wants the knowledge of God experimental rather than reported; Wesley sets the abiding Lord against perishing cities and peoples, and takes the name for infinite power and wisdom and faithfulness and goodness, with the experience of past faithfulness as the ground of confidence.

Ellicott renders the line as enthronement rather than endurance, marks the emphatic pronoun, calls the refuge a citadel into which the persecuted retreat, and derives the verb for seeking from a root meaning to frequent a place, possibly the Temple courts; Delitzsch glosses the refuge as a high steep place out of reach of danger, a figure David knew from his time of persecution, and the oppressed as those broken in pieces and completely crushed.

debates.question: Does the line say that the Lord endures or that he sits enthroned?

sides.position: enthroned: the clause is in close parallelism with the next, that judgment has erected his throne
he shall sit for ever, which a Jewish writer paraphrases as sitting in rest and quiet, and which the Chaldee refers to the Word of the Lord
the point is simply that cities and people may perish while the Lord abides

debates.question: What does a throne prepared for judgment imply?

sides.position: the swiftness and impartiality of divine justice, a court with no delays and no respect of persons
the universality of the judgment, since the word for world covers every country of the habitable earth
that all the dispensations of providence are founded in righteousness and truth

outliers: Gill alone presses the distinction between knowing God notionally or professionally and knowing him affectionately, spiritually and experimentally.
Delitzsch alone derives the word for the oppressed from a root meaning to pulverise, so that the sufferer is overwhelmed to the point of being completely crushed.
themes: a throne that outlasts cities
a court without delays
a citadel for the crushed
a name that works as a watchword

11.pericope_label: Sing praises to the Lord, which dwelleth in Zion: he maketh inquisition for blood and forgetteth not the cry

schools.summary: Henry reads the turn to others as characteristic of praise itself, makes the dwelling in Zion the hinge since the special residence of grace is the church of which Zion was a type, hears the summons running both to David’s subjects and to his neighbours, and expounds the inquisition as a remembering of every drop of innocent blood, with the cry of the humble sealed up among God’s treasures.

Gill allows praise by celebrating God’s perfections and by living to his glory but insists the word here means praise sung in musical notes and sung by the saints in concert, and prefers to read God as searching out the privily shed blood of his saints rather than, with the Arabic, remembering the man who sheds it.

Clarke turns the summons into a rebuke of professing Christians who seldom speak about God because they have nothing to say, and widens the inquisition from the neighbours of Israel to every nation that has made destructive wars for territory or commerce; Wesley identifies Zion as the place of the gracious presence and the people as the heathen nations, and grants the delay while denying the forgetfulness.

Ellicott reads the clause as a reason rather than a condition, identifies the figure as the goel bound by custom to avenge a murdered kinsman, puts the verbs in the past, and prefers the afflicted to the humble while denying that the two forms of the root carry the ethical and physical distinction usually alleged.

debates.question: Whose blood is sought, and by whom?

sides.position: God seeks the blood of his saints, searching out what was privily shed as he searched out Abel’s
God remembers the man who seeks their blood
holders: the Arabic version, reported by John Gill

sides.position: God acts as the goel, the nearest relative bound by custom to avenge the murdered

debates.question: Who is called to account for shed blood?

sides.position: the wicked neighbours of Israel, who used them barbarously and gave no quarter
every nation that has made destructive wars to enlarge its territory or extend its commerce

outliers: Clarke alone turns the verse on his own readers, observing that Christians so called seldom speak about God when they meet, because they have nothing to say.
Gill alone argues from the word itself that the praise meant is sung, the same term being used of the singing of birds.
themes: praise recruited rather than performed alone
a God who inhabits a hill
blood searched for rather than reported
a cry kept among treasures

13.pericope_label: Have mercy upon me, O Lord: lifted from the gates of death to praise in the gates of the daughter of Zion

schools.summary: Spurgeon traces the turn to petition through memory and confidence, admires the prayer as a model that breathes humility and appeals to the right attributes, calls the sentence a little prayer-book holding the soul and marrow of prayer, borrows Trapp on God reserving his hand for a dead lift, and insists the stated object is God’s glory and not relief.

Gill draws the doctrine that a man already called by grace still needs fresh discoveries of pardoning mercy and flees to God rather than the creature, pleading neither dignity nor righteousness nor merit, and measures the promise honestly, since all thy praise can only mean as much of God’s goodness as one man had experience of and could observe.

Clarke sets the verse in the psalm’s argument, where David claims his own part in the maxims he has laid down, and keeps the two sets of gates in one sentence, the open grave against the ordinances by which a soul is helped forward; Wesley reads the second gates as the great assemblies and explains the daughter as the people who meet in the city, cities being as it were mothers to their people.
Delitzsch states the reversal that makes praise possible, that the church has been rescued from death while those who wanted death to overtake it have fallen a prey to death themselves.

debates.question: What are the gates of the daughter of Zion?

sides.position: all the ordinances of God by which the soul is helped forward to heaven, set against the open grave
the great assemblies, the daughter being the people who live and meet together in the city

debates.question: Why is the mercy asked for?

sides.position: for God’s glory, not for relief: the saints want mercy’s diamond so that others may see it flash and admire the giver
because a man called by grace still needs fresh pardon, supply, support and deliverance from enemies inward and outward

outliers: Spurgeon alone divides the psalmist’s whole time between praising and praying, and asks how it could have been spent more profitably.
Gill alone qualifies the vow, since the instances of divine grace are too many to be reckoned up in order in the present state of things.
themes: a prayer short enough to be a book
a dead lift out of a gateway
two sets of gates compared
mercy wanted for someone else to see

15.pericope_label: The heathen are sunk down in the pit that they made: the Lord is known by the judgment which he executeth

schools.summary: Gill marks this as the praise he had promised, occasioned by the destruction of God’s enemies, refuses Kimchi’s Philistines in favour of the antichristian states to be destroyed at Armageddon, traces the metaphor to hunters digging pits for wild beasts, and reads the coming judgment as a retaliation measured out in kind.

Spurgeon finds the justice of the judgment in its economy, since God makes the wicked their own executioners and a snare laboriously made catches its own maker, argues that the punishment of sin is required by what God is and that a ruler who winked at evil would be known to be evil himself, and treats the two untranslated words as a summons to the reader to pause and adjust his heart.

Clarke cautions that not every casualty can properly be called a judgment, since judgment is God’s strange work and leaves no natural causes to which the calamity could legally be attributed, adds that nothing a wicked man does is not against his own interest, and reports the view that the closing words direct the players; Wesley leaves the first of them open between a musical term and a note of attention.

Ellicott recasts the line as two finished clauses, Jehovah hath made himself known, he hath executed judgment, and counts the occurrences of the first untranslated word, which is rendered elsewhere as meditation and as solemn sound, concluding that it probably marks a change in the music or a direction to one part of the orchestra.

debates.question: Are the two untranslated words a musical direction or a call to meditate?

sides.position: probably a change in the music, or with the second word a direction to one part of the orchestra, though both senses are etymologically possible
either a musical term or a note of attention, the matter deserving consideration
both: meditate on this and mark it well, though some take the words for a direction to the players
a summons to the reader to pause, consider and tune his instrument

debates.question: Why is God known by the judgment he executes?

sides.position: because his holiness and abhorrence of sin are displayed in judging, as a ruler reveals his nature by what he punishes
because the judgment on antichrist will make his name and perfections known in all the earth
because when judgment is executed there are no natural causes to which such calamities can be attributed, so his mind is plainly seen

outliers: Spurgeon alone lists the self-destructions that parallel the pit, with drunkards killing themselves, prodigals beggaring themselves and the envious eating their own hearts.
Clarke alone notes that the wicked man takes more pains to destroy his soul than the righteous man takes to have his saved.
themes: a hunter in his own pitfall
judgment as self-disclosure
two words left untranslated
a retaliation measured in kind

17.pericope_label: The wicked shall be turned into hell: yet the needy shall not alway be forgotten

schools.summary: Gill rejects the rendering return to the dust on the ground that it is common to the righteous as well, takes the place named for the place of torment to which the wicked go at once and are remanded in soul and body after the judgment, and keeps both halves of the promise to the needy, who are never forgotten yet may seem so for a long time.

Spurgeon spells out who is caught by the warning, the moral who are not devout and the honest who are not prayerful among them, holds that forgetfulness looks a small sin yet brings eternal wrath, and answers the fear of the needy by setting divine assurance against Satan’s word that their hope shall perish.

Clarke keeps the traditional sense of the verb and presses its emphasis, distinguishes forgetting from ignorance and turns the warning on his own reader, and accounts for delayed deliverance by the greater confusion of enemies and the greater manifestation of mercy; Wesley defines forgetting as not regarding God nor his precepts nor his threatenings.

Ellicott calls the received rendering most unfortunate, since the verb is to return and the destination the grave or the unseen world, ties the verse to the previous one because the wicked bring about their own destruction, and notes that the negative in the next verse stands emphatically at the head and governs both clauses; Delitzsch reads the prayer as growing more confident because an act of judgment has already been witnessed.

sides.position: they return to the grave, that is to dust or to the unseen world; the received rendering is most unfortunate and the verbs may even be imperative
to the place of torment where devils and damned spirits are, since returning to dust is common to righteous and wicked alike
headlong into hell, down into hell, the original being very emphatic

debates.question: Who are the forgetters of God?

sides.position: nations and individuals who know God and are nevertheless unmindful of him in their designs and works
those who do not regard God, nor his precepts, nor his threatenings
the moral who are not devout, the honest who are not prayerful, the benevolent who are not believing, the amiable who are not converted — far more numerous than the profligate

outliers: Clarke alone breaks off to address his reader directly, asking whether he is forgetful of his Maker and of him who died for him.
Gill alone measures the seeming forgetfulness by the periods of the holy city trodden under foot and the witnesses prophesying in sackcloth.
themes: a verb that decides a doctrine
forgetting counted as wickedness
a negative that governs two clauses
waiting that is not in vain

19.pericope_label: Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail: that the nations may know themselves to be but men

schools.summary: Gill reads the summons as double, to the destruction of the enemies and the salvation of the people, and keeps the received reading of the last petition, praying that fear be injected into a bold and fearless generation who neither fear God nor regard men, as it will be at the destruction of Babylon.

Spurgeon makes prayer the believer’s weapon of war and God the ally who lies in ambush until faith cries Arise, warns that he who is now all tenderness will show no compassion to those who had no tears of repentance, finds it astonishing that men grow vain enough to deny being men, and closes by recommending the psalm be read again as the triumphal hymn of the Redeemer.

Clarke renders the last petition as a prayer for a teacher to be placed among them, citing the versions and two older English renderings against the reading fear, makes the lesson evangelical so that the Gentiles learn by preaching that they need the salvation Christ provided, and closes by quoting Horsley’s three-part division of the psalm.

Ellicott sharpens the petition to let not mere man be defiant, states the textual difficulty in the last verse, reports that the Greek and the Latin and the Syriac read place a lawgiver over them and that Hitzig conjectured set a guard upon them, and takes the received text to mean put a terror upon them.

debates.question: What is asked for in the final petition?

sides.position: a teacher or legislator placed among them, which is the reading of every version but one and was caught by two older English renderings
a terror put upon them, that is, such a proof of power as to trouble and subdue them, though the Greek, Latin and Syriac read lawgiver and Hitzig conjectured a guard
fear injected into a fearless generation, as at the destruction of Babylon

debates.question: How is the psalm put together?

sides.position: in three parts of falling temperature: a prophetic song of victory, then triumph mixed with supplication, then cool assertion and prayer
as the triumphal hymn of the Redeemer, laying the glory of his victories at his Father’s feet

outliers: Spurgeon alone piles up the instances that leave a man only a man, the wealth of Croesus and the wisdom of Solon and the power of Alexander together.
Clarke alone reports the older English renderings that set a schoolmaster over the nations and a bringer of law above them.
themes: prayer used as a weapon
a lawgiver or a terror
crowns that leave their wearers men
a psalm that cools as it ends
